clue.text: Cameron, perhaps fated to spill daughter's secret

parts.note: Cameron is one of the Scottish clans, so it stands for the general word clan

indicators.note: to spill something is to let it fall out, so a letter drops out of the word before it

parts.note: fated means destined
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone's fate is to leak a daughter's private information, with a former prime minister named Cameron the suggested culprit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cameron, perhaps' tempts you towards David Cameron the politician, but it is the Scottish clan. DESTINED loses its final D.
explanation.definitionFit: Something clandestine is kept hidden or done covertly, a close synonym of secret.

clue.text: About to probe Chanel, the French globally-recognised brand

indicators.note: to probe is to poke into something, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Coco Chanel was the French fashion designer, so her first name is taken
CA is short for circa, Latin for about
la is a French word for the

explanation.surface: Coco Chanel's fashion house is presented as a world-famous French label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chanel' points to the designer's nickname; the abbreviation for 'about' goes into the middle of it rather than at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: The fizzy drink's name is among the most widely known trademarks on earth.

clue.text: Marginal difference causing concern

indicators.note: a difference here is a change in the letters, so the word beside it is rearranged

explanation.surface: A slim margin between two results is cause for worry, like a close election poll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marginal difference' reads as one phrase, but 'difference' is the anagram signal working on 'Marginal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarming things are worrying or frightening, so they cause concern.

clue.text: Summer party Ms Summers set up

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the letters are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: Ann Summers is a British chain of lingerie and adult shops, named as if a woman

explanation.surface: A summer party is hosted by a woman named Ms Summers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ann Summers is a British high-street chain of lingerie shops. The definition points to the disco singer Donna Summer, whose first name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The disco star known as Summer had the given name Donna, so her surname clues her first name.

clue.text: 24ct, very aged cover, good lining

indicators.note: a lining sits inside something, so these letters go within the others

parts.note: so means very, as in so tired
aged means old
a lid is a cover

explanation.surface: A description of a very old object with a cover and a fine lining, valued at 24 carats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lining' puts the cover and good inside 'very aged', which splits between its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold of 24 carats is pure, with no alloy, which is what solid gold means.

clue.text: Suffer a bit of pain currently

indicators.note: a bit of means only a part of the words that follow is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Someone is currently experiencing a little pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'paIN CURrently'.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a loss or penalty is to suffer it or bring it on oneself.

clue.text: English charitable foundation endlessly preserves old Europeans

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a trust is a body set up to manage a charitable fund
cans are tins that preserve food; to can is to preserve

explanation.surface: An English charity keeps the remains of ancient European peoples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preserves' looks like the verb governing the next words, but it gives CANS, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Etruscans were an ancient people of central Italy, so old Europeans.

clue.text: Dinghy for one dropping off old fly-by-night?

indicators.note: dropping off means a letter falls away from the word

parts.note: a dinghy is an example of a boat

explanation.surface: A dinghy loses its elderly passenger, who turns out to be a dodgy character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly-by-night' usually means an unreliable person; here, with the question mark, it is read literally as a creature that flies at night.
explanation.definitionFit: A bat is a nocturnal flying mammal, so it literally flies by night.

clue.text: Cliff Richard's last after Sandie Shaw on the radio … yeah, weird

indicators.note: after places the letter it governs behind the rest

parts.note: the singer's name spoken sounds like sandy shore, which is a beach

indicators.note: weird means odd or strange, so the letters of the word beside it are scrambled
last means only the final letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Pop names gathered as Cliff Richard follows Sandie Shaw on the radio, and a listener replies with a puzzled yeah.
explanation.walkthrough: Cliff Richard and Sandie Shaw are 1960s British pop singers, but 'Cliff' is the definition. 'Weird' scrambles 'yeah' to YHEA; 'after' puts Richard's last letter at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Beachy Head is a famous chalk cliff on the south coast of England, near Eastbourne.

clue.text: Warning nurse about hospital

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: to nurse a patient is to treat them
H is the standard abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A caution is given to a nurse about something at the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurse' looks like a noun but works as the verb treat.
explanation.definitionFit: A threat can be a menacing indication of danger, so a warning.

clue.text: ITV say Detective Charlie McCluskey's retiring

parts.note: Charlie Chan is a fictional Chinese-American detective

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Len McCluskey was general secretary of the Unite trade union

explanation.surface: A TV network reports that a detective called Charlie McCluskey is leaving the force.
explanation.walkthrough: ITV is a British commercial television network. 'Charlie McCluskey' looks like one person's name, but it splits into two people.
explanation.definitionFit: ITV is an example of a television station, which is a broadcasting channel.

clue.text: Pirate singing bawdy sea shanty

indicators.note: singing means the words are voiced, so their sound gives the entry

parts.note: bawdy means coarse, and a shanty is a song, an air

explanation.surface: A pirate belts out a rude sailors' song.
explanation.walkthrough: COARSE AIR, said out loud, gives the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A corsair was a privateer or pirate, especially on the Barbary Coast.

clue.text: Naval officer to requisition one leaving base?

indicators.note: leaving means a letter departs from the word

parts.note: to commandeer is to requisition, to seize for official use
one of the two letters E in the longer word is the one that goes

explanation.surface: Someone takes over a ship or vehicle as an officer departs from the naval base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a naval base; with the question mark it hints the officer leaves base, a playful touch. One of COMMANDEER's two Es leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A commander is a naval rank just below captain.

clue.text: School with American vowel sound?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a school uses American pronunciation of vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: The schwa is the neutral, unstressed vowel heard in the first syllable of about.

clue.text: Neil got ugly freckle

indicators.note: ugly suggests something misshapen, so the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A man named Neil developed an unattractive freckle.
explanation.definitionFit: Lentigo is the medical term for a small pigmented spot on the skin, much like a freckle.

clue.text: Fiancée regularly skipped introduction to fairy tale — beyond words!

indicators.note: letters are regularly skipped, so every other letter is taken
an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: a fable is a tale, often with a moral

explanation.surface: A bride-to-be skipped through a fairy-tale romance too wonderful to describe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly skipped' takes the even letters of 'Fiancée', I, N, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineffable describes what is too great or extreme to be expressed in speech.

clue.text: Rump steak's prime cut to swallow

indicators.note: the prime cut is the top portion, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: to swallow food is to eat it

explanation.surface: A butcher's prime rump steak, ready to be eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rump steak' reads as one cut of meat, but 'Rump' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rump and seat are both informal words for the buttocks.

clue.text: They traffic sheepskin boots in all sizes all over Queens

indicators.note: in a down clue, all over means stacked on top of what follows
in places the boots within the sizes

parts.note: S, M and L are the clothing sizes small, medium and large
Ugg is a well-known brand of sheepskin boot
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, a queen; two of them are ERS

explanation.surface: Fashion dealers sell sheepskin boots in every size throughout Queens, the New York borough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queens' looks like the New York borough but means two monarchs. 'In' sets the boots between medium and large; 'all over' stacks the result above the queens.
explanation.definitionFit: Smugglers move goods illegally, which is to traffic in them.

clue.text: Court impounding cheapo plastic vase from France

indicators.note: impounding means seizing and holding, so one piece encloses the other
plastic means mouldable, so the letters can be reshaped

explanation.surface: A court seizes a cheap plastic vase imported from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' looks like the vase's material but scrambles 'cheapo' to ACHEPO; 'impounding' has the court abbreviation hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache-pot is a French ornamental container for hiding a plant pot, a kind of vase.

clue.text: Tyrannical Democrat in charge detaining tortured poets

indicators.note: detaining means holding something inside
tortured means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An oppressive political leader locks up and tortures poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tortured' scrambles 'poets' to ESPOT, and 'detaining' has the two abbreviations hold it, one at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is an absolute ruler, so despotic behaviour is tyrannical.

clue.text: See 7
Eclipse London-bound coach

parts.note: travelling up is the traditional British term for going towards London
a stagecoach, or stage, was a horse-drawn passenger coach

explanation.surface: A coach heads for London during an eclipse.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you go up to London from anywhere else, so UP means London-bound.
explanation.definitionFit: To upstage someone is to outshine or overshadow them, which is to eclipse them.

clue.text: UK releases my work — I'm not welcome here

indicators.note: to work material is to shape it, so the letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A British record label puts out an album, and a migrant laments not being welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Releases' and 'work' suggest a music label's output, but 'work' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A person seeking refuge often feels unwanted in a new country, so might say these words.

clue.text: See 20
Will the writer — asks Connery — store books here?

indicators.note: Sean Connery's famous pronunciation turns an s into sh, so the name is said in his voice

parts.note: Will Self is an English novelist

explanation.surface: Sean Connery asks whether the author will keep his books here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a verb, but it is the first name of the novelist Will Self; Connery's slushy s turns SELF into SHELF.
explanation.definitionFit: Books are kept on a horizontal board fixed to a wall or in a bookcase.

clue.text: One anchored at sea sparks up joint

parts.note: to spark up a cigarette is to light it
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Someone sparks up a cannabis joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a cannabis cigarette but is the body joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A lightship is a vessel moored in position to serve as a lighthouse.

clue.text: Chap stowing away boy-king?

parts.note: a lad is a boy
ER is Edwardus Rex, the abbreviation for King Edward

explanation.surface: A man stows away a boy king, as if smuggling a young monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To lade is to load cargo, so a person doing that is a loader stowing goods away.

clue.text: Bottomless sea motif

indicators.note: in a down clue, bottomless means the lowest, last letter is removed

parts.note: the Med is the Mediterranean Sea, here with its article

explanation.surface: A design motif of an unfathomably deep sea.
explanation.walkthrough: THE MED loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is a recurring idea or subject, the same thing as a motif.

clue.text: Produce bake with light crust and a very soggy bottom!

indicators.note: a crust encloses a filling, so these letters go around the others

parts.note: an LED is a light-emitting diode, a light

indicators.note: to produce something is to make it, so the letters are made into a new order

explanation.surface: Baking advice, as on a TV baking contest: a light crust risks a very soggy bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'soggy bottom' is the dreaded underbaked pastry base on The Great British Bake Off. 'Produce' scrambles 'bake' to AKEB, and 'crust' wraps the light round it.
explanation.definitionFit: The bed of a lake is its floor beneath the water, a thoroughly wet bottom.

clue.text: Optical illusion on a butterfly's wing?

definitions.text: Optical illusion on a butterfly's wing?

parts.words: Optical illusion on a butterfly's wing?
parts.note: a wing marking that looks like a watching eye to scare off predators

explanation.surface: A pattern on a butterfly that tricks the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Many butterflies carry a round marking resembling an eye, which deters birds.

clue.text: Tarnish articulate BBC politics presenter

indicators.note: articulate means spoken clearly, so the name is said out loud

parts.note: Andrew, the Scottish journalist who hosted a BBC Sunday morning politics show for many years

explanation.surface: A smear campaign against an eloquent political broadcaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulate' looks like praise for the presenter but is the signal that the name is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to spoil or damage it, which is to tarnish it.

clue.text: Secret coup I organised, being fixated on sovereignty

indicators.note: organised means arranged, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A plotter confesses to having organised a hidden coup to protect national sovereignty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret' looks like part of the definition, but it is in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Opponents of deeper EU integration typically focus on national self-government.
